Encode a DateTime into Eight Characters with base32 in Rust

July 2026

Character Dates

This is how I convert a timestamp into an eight character string. I use the strings to make IDs and the file/folder tree for my blog posts. That way I don't have to worry about trying to come up with folder names (or changing them if I change the title of a post).

The Code

Rust

Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "base32_timestamp"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
anyhow = "1.0.104"
base32 = "0.5.1"
chrono = "0.4.45"
src/main.rs
use anyhow::{Result, anyhow};
use base32::Alphabet;
use chrono::{DateTime, FixedOffset, Utc};

fn main() -> Result<()> {
  let dt1 =
    DateTime::parse_from_rfc3339("2026-07-17T10:30:00-04:00")?;

  let encoded1 = encode_base32_datetime(&dt1);
  let decoded1 = decode_base32_datetime(&encoded1);

  let dt2 =
    DateTime::parse_from_rfc3339("2026-07-17T10:36:00-04:00")?;

  let encoded2 = encode_base32_datetime(&dt2);
  let decoded2 = decode_base32_datetime(&encoded2);

  println!("{}", encoded1);
  println!("{}", encoded2);
  println!("{}", decoded1?.to_rfc3339());
  println!("{}", decoded2?.to_rfc3339());

  Ok(())
}

fn encode_base32_datetime(
  datetime: &DateTime<FixedOffset>
) -> String {
  let bytes = &datetime.timestamp().to_be_bytes()[3..8];
  base32::encode(Alphabet::Crockford, bytes).to_lowercase()
}

fn decode_base32_datetime(dt: &str) -> Result<DateTime<Utc>> {
  let five_bytes = base32::decode(Alphabet::Crockford, dt)
    .ok_or(anyhow!("Could not decode datetime"))?;
  let mut buf = [0u8; 8];
  buf[3..8].copy_from_slice(&five_bytes);
  let ts = i64::from_be_bytes(buf);
  DateTime::from_timestamp(ts, 0)
    .ok_or(anyhow!("Could not decode timestamp"))
}

Output

01n5mf38
01n5mfeg
2026-07-17T14:30:00+00:00
2026-07-17T14:36:00+00:00

Outro

Nothing fancy. But, super useful when it comes to not having to think about how to name things.

-a

Endnotes

  • This example originally used the data_encoding Rust crate with BASE32_NOPAD. The timestamps were encoded but the resulting strings did not sort in the same order as the timestamps they represented (letters come before numbers which breaks the order).

    I switched to using the base32 Rust crate that provides the Crockford Alphabet. The strings sort the same way as their timestamps with that setup.

  • The dates to in with a timezone but come out as Utc (e.g. 2026-07-17T10:30:00-04:00 becomes 2026-07-17T14:30:00+00:00. That's expected since the Unix epoch timestamp that's used for the encoding doesn't contain time zone info.

  • The encoded timestamp has a resolution of one second. That's all I need for creating blog post IDs (which is what I'm using this for). I want them to be 8 characters which base32 can handle when it's only dealing with seconds. If you need millisecond or finder granularity more characters would be required for the base32 value.

    The reason I'm limiting the encoded values to 8 characters it to make the URLs somewhat approachable (e.g. /blog/01/n5/mf/38/). Or, at least, not as wild as using something like a UUID (v7) that give you milliseconds but is way longer and looks like this:

      fb2a482b-3694-4d8f-a2ed-402077fe97c4

  • I had been truncating a KSUID to get the characters. I switched to doing it with base32 since I'm not using the randomness that provides.

  • Some details on base32 encoding:

    • It uses 32 characters where each one represents 5 bits.

    • 5 bits x 8 characters = 40 bits of data.

    • 40 bits (2^40) represents a little over 1 trillion values.

    • At 1 second per value, the 40 bits represents about 34,000 years. More than enough to cover the expected time I'll be posting on my blog.

  • The .to_be_bytes()[3..8] call keeps the output lined up chronologically (by making it Big Endian, which I only half way understand), and strips of the first few bits from the byte which aren't needed.
